never: Never state a character's emotion outright when a concrete object, gesture, or sound can carry it instead.
Never resolve the story neatly or grant the character the action they long for; honour the paralysis.
Never use vague or generic settings; an unnamed street or city betrays the whole method.
Never raise the emotional volume, melodramatise, or editorialise about how sad it all is.
Never reach for ornate, abstract, or self-consciously literary diction over the plain true word.
Never break into the character's head with explanatory tags like 'he felt' or 'she realised' when free indirect drift will do.
Never explain the meaning of the closing image; let it stand unannotated.
Never let the narrator mock the character or condescend; pity and irony must stay in balance.
always: Always name the specific Dublin place, street, church, or station that grounds the scene.
Always build by accretion, chaining clauses with 'and' until small things accumulate into weight.
Always let cold, damp, grey light, or a failing lamp do the work of mood.
Always slide into free indirect discourse, voicing the character's own idiom and self-deceptions.
Always end on a held stillness or a diminishing image rather than a conclusion.
Always place a small physical gesture at the emotional crisis to carry what cannot be said.
Always let a memory of a lost chance surface and then sink back unnamed.
Always keep the surface calm so that feeling presses up from beneath.
